records.label: Hinenosho manor land-clearance and irrigation sequence
records.interval_semantics: Physical land-use sequence only; no population or equilibrium interval is reported.
pressure_evidence: Farris (2006, p. 134) reports only 12 cho of cropland after the 1234 famine, rising to nearly 33 cho by 1316 and almost 54 cho by 1417.
The Japan Heritage Hinenosho archive describes the 1309 land survey and detailed village/pond/paddy maps, and a 2.75 km Yukawa watercourse built for slope and paddy irrigation.
The sequence is evidence of land development and water investment after subsistence stress, not proof that the 1316 population was at a Malthusian ceiling.
shock_flags: 1316 map/survey date is not a census
Estate boundary is a manor, not an EU5 province polygon
records.food_regime: wet rice, wheat/dry fields, ponds, forest products, and local irrigation
records.boundary_description: Hinenosho manor (present-day Izumisano area), including Hineno and Iriyamada villages; no verified EU5 boundary selector.
records.notes: Useful rural pressure/technology validation case. No defensible population interval, saturation fraction, or exact EU5 crosswalk; never use as a fitted target.

records.label: Fayyum Dilya canal village cluster in al-Nabulusi's 1245 survey
records.interval_semantics: Canal-cluster hydraulic and settlement evidence only; fiscal records do not enumerate total people or an equilibrium capacity.
records.metric_semantics: Village counts and clan/canal overlap from Rapoport & Shahar (2012, pp. 25-26; Map 1/Map 3), not population counts.
pressure_evidence: Rapoport & Shahar (2012, pp. 25-26, Maps 1 and 3) find near-complete overlap between some clans and branch canals, indicating locally organized water rights and food production.
The Dilya and Tanabṭawayh clusters were multi-village irrigation units; water and maintenance were coordinated across villages rather than supplied by a distant food market.
The evidence identifies local hydraulic constraints and collective maintenance, but gives no population interval or saturation fraction.
shock_flags: Canal-cluster fiscal values can aggregate multiple villages
Fayyum GIS-to-EU5 boundary has not been digitized
records.food_regime: gravity-irrigated cereals, legumes, sugar, livestock, and local canal agriculture
records.boundary_description: Dilya/Tanabṭawayh canal village clusters in the Fayyum depression; historical village polygons are not available in the EU5 geometry inventory.
records.notes: Strong local-food and water-rights diagnostic, but no demographic label. Keep blocked until a village population source and GIS crosswalk are independently established.

records.label: Fayyum Nile-flow shortage and village maintenance pressure
records.interval_semantics: Hydraulic stress and maintenance evidence only; no population or saturation interval is available.
records.metric_semantics: Hydraulic-flow and dredging-tool figures from al-Nabulusi as analyzed by Rapoport & Shahar (2012, pp. 10 and 25-26); these are not population counts.
pressure_evidence: Rapoport & Shahar (2012, p. 10) report that the Bahr Yusuf historically flowed eight months and was dry four, while in al-Nabulusi's time this was reversed, directly documenting water scarcity.
The same study (pp. 25-26) reports 104 dredging-tool units assessed against Fayyum villages and 95 actually supplied; local peasants gathered to clear the canal mouth before inundation.
This is a concrete local production constraint and collective response, but it cannot be converted to a population ceiling without demographic evidence.
shock_flags: Fayyum-wide physical system is not an exact EU5 settlement boundary
records.food_regime: Nile basin irrigation, wheat, barley, legumes, sugar, livestock, and fisheries
records.boundary_description: Fayyum depression hydraulic system and its villages; no audited EU5 polygon crosswalk.
records.notes: Use as a physical water-stress regression case only. It must not become a population label or regional multiplier.
